newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank, industry urge ambitious tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank, industry urge ambitious tax reform.

text.p: Germany's powerful central bank and leading industrial executives on Sunday strongly urged Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition to carry out a more comprehensive overhaul of the country's tax system.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said a thorough reform of the income tax system was sorely needed to keep companies from moving jobs abroad and create the conditions for economic growth at home and improve state finances.
"Our tax system -- and that is one of the problems -- is no longer competitive enough. But we live in a world in which there is competition between systems," he told Hesse Radio.

Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) passed tax reform bills for 1998 and 1999 in the lower house last week, but the bills are expected to be blocked by the opposition-controlled upper house this week.
The government tax reform seeks a net tax reduction of around 30 billion marks ($17.3 billion) by cutting lowering income tax rates.

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of Lower Saxony and a leading Social Democratic (SPD) contender to challenge Kohl in 1998 elections, said at the weekend that there was no reason for the SPD to support a broad tax reform before the election.
Rather than support Bonn's plan, the SPD could wait and, if elected, carry out its own reform that would focus on providing relief for those who form the bulwark of society, he said.
"That is not the millionaires, but millions of people with annual incomes between 60,000 marks and 120,000 marks who every day create our gross national product," he said.

Hermann Otto Solms, a powerful FDP behind-the-scenes mover and shaker, told the news weekly Der Spiegel that differences between the FDP and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) had the coalition walking a fine line.
"We are in difficult territory," he said in an interview to be published on Monday.

One bone of contension between Kohl's CDU and the FDP is an earlier decision to cut the solidarity tax -- a surcharge on income tax bills to finance German unification -- next year. Many CDU deputies would rather postpone the cut.
"Whoever retreats from lowering the solidarity surcharge breaks his promise to taxpayers. The FDP is not willing to do this," said Solms.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber said it was crucial to lower the top income tax rate, now 53 percent, but suggested that the net tax cut could be lower than planned.
"I would be happy if we got 15 to 20 billion marks," he told German Radio.
German industry has come down hard on the legislation.

The Federation of German Industry said the bills increase taxes on companies by some 13 billion marks next year and with the future of Kohl's weary coalition uncertain industry is sceptical that tax relief will come in 1999 as promised.

Bernd Pischetsrieder, chairman of luxury car maker Bayerische Motoren Werke AG, told the news weekly Der Spiegel that industry criticism of the government was not a call for a change of power in Bonn.
But he added that the government's tax reform lacked a coherent overriding concept and it failed to correct faults in the system or to put Germany on track for global competition in the next century.
"They are only plugging holes," he said.

"In our country we need to set a course for the coming decades and not only in regard to tax policies. But we are only concerned with that which is tactically necessary or opportune in the short term instead of acting strategically."
-- William.Boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
($ = 1.738 German Marks)
